extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophy of language, and scientific authors
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for designing and using a philosophical/scientific language: how terms should be coined, fixed, and employed to promote precision, induction, and clear descriptive recording of observations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms must convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: That its terms shall each of them convey a determinate and unmistakable meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental requisite for a language fitted to investigate truth; discussed with examples of semantic drift and loss of precision (e.g., 'pagan', 'villain'). Emphasizes resisting ambiguous connotation and fixing meanings for philosophical/scientific discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: No important meaning without a word (vocabulary completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no important meaning without its word. Whatever we have occasion to think of often, and for scientific purposes, ought to have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treated under three heads: (1) descriptive terminology for observations, (2) names for general conceptions needed in induction, (3) a nomenclature giving names for Kinds. Ensures nothing important lacks a concise label.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate descriptive terminology for recording observations
rubrics_metrics.description: There ought to be all such names, as are needful for making such a record of individual observations that the words of the record shall exactly show what fact it is which has been observed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical/descriptive terms must be fixed by convention and, when possible, associated immediately with the perception (e.g., color names like 'apple-green', botanical terms: calyx, corolla, stamens). Elementary sensations cannot be defined and must be learnt via direct experience or exemplars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names for results of abstraction (terms for inductive concepts)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the comparison of a set of phenomena leads to the recognition in them of some common circumstance ... this new conception should have a name appropriated to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concise names for abstractions promote perspicuity and make ideas memorable (examples: 'limit', 'momentum', 'delegation vs representation'). Naming facilitates thought, recall, and communication of new concepts discovered by induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nomenclature: a name for every Kind
rubrics_metrics.description: There shall be a name for every Kind. By a Kind we mean classes distinguished by an indefinite multitude of properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kinds (e.g., 'horse', 'animal') require names because members share many properties; nomenclature complements descriptive terminology and ensures that significant natural classes have compact labels for predicates and further inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix technical term meanings by convention and perception
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of [descriptive] technical terms can be fixed in the first instance only by convention, and can be made intelligible only by presenting to the senses that which the terms are to signify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teach technical terms through direct exemplars (e.g., color swatches, botanical specimens). Rely on convention rather than vague common-language associations to ensure immediate recognition and avoid insecure conjectural meanings (Whewell quoted).

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity and compact names improve clarity of reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: When a thing has to be often spoken of, there are more reasons than the saving of time and space, for speaking of it in the most concise manner possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short, compact names concentrate attention on relations (mathematical/abstract examples) and prevent distraction by component descriptions; aids discovery and transmission of complex ideas (examples: 'limit', 'momentum').

rubrics_metrics.name: Define words according to current usage when change is irrevocable
rubrics_metrics.description: The logician ... should submit to them with a good grace when they are irrevocably effected, and if a definition is necessary, define the word according to its new meaning; retaining the former as a second signification, if it is needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: when semantic shift has occurred irreversibly, acknowledge and define the new sense for clarity in philosophical discourse; preserve prior sense where feasible for technical/philosophical use. Logicians cannot control popular meanings but can clarify and formalize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against degeneration of language by ignorant misuse
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalization of names through ignorant misuse is a real source of alterations in the language; vulgarisms ... are daily depriving the English language of valuable modes of expressing thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be wary of common misuse turning precise terms into vague or inverted meanings (examples: 'transpire' used as 'to happen'; 'aggravating' for 'provoking'; misuse of 'alone', 'predicate'/'predict', 'eliminate'). Such corruptions narrow expressive resources and force circumlocution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid translator-induced semantic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Blunders of translators can produce permanent deterioration in the language by associating foreign senses with native words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French 'demander' rendered as 'to demand' leading to shift from 'demand' to mere 'ask'; 'transaction' used for French 'compromis'. Translators should preserve distinctions to prevent cross-language loss of terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise, sometimes numerical, definitions when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Other characters ... are conveyed with like precision: Color by means of a classified scale of colors ... Mohs improved ... by giving a numerical scale of hardness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where properties admit, introduce arbitrarily precise or numerical criteria (e.g., botanical terms with numeric thresholds, Mohs hardness scale) to fix meanings and enable clear differentiation between cases (examples: bilobate vs bifid, siliqua vs silicula).
